and the Servant is directed, not only to invite, but to bring them in,' as otherwise they might naturally shrink from coming to such a feast.

luke-14-parable.caution: Both are interpretations of the parable, not of first-century table custom.

luke-14-parable.text: Smith's Dictionary describes the customs of a formal meal. The principal meal was taken after sunset, and the word 'supper' in Luke 14:12 is, it says, more properly 'dinner'. Guests reclined on couches arranged on three sides of a square, with the fourth side left open for servants, and 'a single dish' into which each guest dipped his hand. On state occasions the guests were invited beforehand, and 'on the day of the feast a second invitation was issued to those that were bidden', and places were settled according to rank.

evidence.quote: The Jews rather followed the custom that prevails among the Bedouins, and made their principal meal after sunset
The ordinary arrangement of the couches was in three sides of a square, the fourth being left open for the servants to bring up the dishes.
the guests were previously invited, (Esther 5:8; Matthew 22:3) and on the day of the feast a second invitation was issued to those that were bidden.
The places of the guests were settled according to their respective rand, (Genesis 43:33; Mark 12:39)

luke-14-parable.caution: Smith's is describing Jewish practice in general from the Old and New Testaments. 'Rand' is an OCR error for 'rank' in the file.

luke-14-parable.text: On the poor at feasts, Smith's Dictionary says the poor among the Hebrews were much favoured: they were allowed to glean, to gather what the land produced in the year it was not tilled, and 'they were also invited to feasts', citing Deuteronomy 14:29 and 26:12. Jesus's advice to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame and the blind thus rests on a pattern already in the Law.

evidence.quote: The poor among the Hebrews were much favored.
They were also invited to feasts.

luke-14-parable.caution: The last sentence of the text is the writer's link between Smith's account and Luke 14:13; Smith's does not mention Luke 14.

jeremiah-31.text: Matthew Henry heads chapter 31 'Joyful Return from Captivity' and dates it about 594 BC. On verse 8 he says many of those returning are unfit for travel, yet the blind and the lame shall come: they will have such good will for the journey that they shall not make their blindness and lameness an excuse for staying where they are. Of the pregnant women he says the same: when God calls, we must not plead inability, for he who calls us will help us.
jeremiah-31.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Jeremiah 31

evidence.quote: Joyful Return from Captivity. (b. c. 594.)

The blind and the lame shall come; such a good-will shall they have to their journey, and such a good heart upon it, that they shall not make their blindness and lameness an excuse for staying where they are.
Note, When God calls we must not plead any inability to come; for he that calls us will help us, will strengthen us.

jeremiah-31.caution: Henry's reading. He treats the blind and lame as real travellers, but his lesson ('do not plead inability') is a sermon point that a blind reader may or may not welcome; consider whether to publish it.

jeremiah-31.text: Matthew Henry notes that their companions will be ready to help them, will be eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, and he cites Job 29:15; but, above all, he says, their God will help them, 'let none plead that he is blind who has God for his guide, or lame who has God for his strength.' So Henry sees two kinds of help on the road home: the help of fellow travellers and the guidance of God.
jeremiah-31.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Jeremiah 31

evidence.quote: There companions will be ready to help them, will be eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, as good Christians ought to be to one another in their travels heavenward, Job xxix. 15.
But, above all, their God will help them; and let none plead that he is blind who has God for his guide, or lame who has God for his strength.

jeremiah-31.caution: Henry's reading. Verse 9 says only that God will lead them by streams of water in a straight way where they will not stumble; the companions are Henry's addition.

jeremiah-31.text: For the road itself, Matthew Henry takes verse 9 as a promise answering each hazard of a long journey home. If the country is dry and thirsty, God will cause them to walk by rivers of water. If it is a wilderness with no road or track, God will cause them to walk in a straight way which they shall not miss. If it is a rough and rocky country, they shall not stumble. He also reads 'with weeping and with supplications' as weeping for sin as they are delivered from captivity.
jeremiah-31.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Jeremiah 31

evidence.quote: Is the country they pass through dry and thirsty? I will cause them to walk by the rivers of waters, not the waters of a land-flood, which fail in summer.
They shall come with weeping and with supplications, weeping for sin, supplication for pardon
Is it a wilderness where there is no road, no track? I will cause them to walk in a straight way, which they shall not miss. Is it a rough and rocky country? Yet they shall not stumble.

jeremiah-31.caution: Henry's paraphrase; the verse itself names only streams of water and a straight way where they will not stumble.

jeremiah-31.text: On the larger setting, Matthew Henry says God will again take Israel into covenant with himself and that the watchmen on Mount Ephraim will call people to go up to Zion; he says the promise was to be fully accomplished 'in the days of the Messiah'. The 1915 Bible encyclopedia describes chapters 30 to 33 of Jeremiah as the 'Book of Comfort', and says predictions of restoration became more frequent in Jeremiah during the siege and afterwards.
jeremiah-31.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Jeremiah 31; International Standard Bible Encyclopaedia (1915), entry 'Jeremiah'

evidence.quote: God here assures his people, I. That he will again take them into a covenant relation to himself
the watchmen upon Mount Ephraim, that are set to stand sentinel there, to give notice of the approach of the enemy, finding that all is very quiet
This promise was to have its full accomplishment in the days of the Messiah, when the gospel should be preached to all these countries
such predictions are Jeremiah Jeremy, Ep. of THE INTERNATIONAL STANDARD BIBLE ENCYCLOPAEDIA 15(H) more frequent (cf 23 1 fT; 24 (if; 47 2-7; and in tin' "Book of Comfort," chs 30-33).

jeremiah-31.caution: The ISBE quotation includes a running head from the OCR; the text should not reproduce it. Henry's Messianic reading is one of several the shelf does not set against each other.

job-29-15.text: Matthew Henry reads 'eyes to the blind' in Job 29:15 as advice, not as help with the physical lack of sight. In his view Job counselled and advised those who did not know what to do, and was feet to the lame by helping with money and friends those who knew what to do but not how to do it. He adds that we best help people by helping them in the very thing in which they are lacking, and that since we may become blind or lame ourselves we should pity and help those who are.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Job 29

evidence.quote: I was eyes to the blind, counselling and advising those for the best that knew not what to do, and feet to the lame, assisting those with money and friends that knew what they should do, but knew not how to compass it.

Those we best help whom we help out in that very thing wherein they are defective and most need help. We may come to be blind or lame ourselves, and therefore should pity and succour those that are so

job-29-15.caution: Commentary of the early 18th century. Henry reads the verse figuratively (the 'blind' are those without direction); he does not discuss a person who is physically blind.

job-29-15.text: In his comment on the healing of the two blind men in Matthew 9, Matthew Henry draws exactly the line Brian asks about. Job, he says, was eyes to the blind, standing to them instead of eyes, but could not give eyes to the blind, and he notes that opening the eyes of the blind is spoken of as God's own prerogative. Seen this way, being someone's eyes and giving someone sight are different things, and only the second is called God's work.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Matthew 9

evidence.quote: Job was eyes to the blind (Job xxix. 15); was to them instead of eyes, but he could not give eyes to the blind.
for it is God's prerogative to open the eyes of the blind (Ps. cxlvi. 8); he makes the seeing eye, Exod. iv. 11.

job-29-15.caution: This is the only place on the shelf that explicitly separates serving as eyes from giving eyes. It is one sentence, and Henry's point there is about Christ's power, not about how a blind person experiences being guided.

job-29-15.text: Matthew Henry uses the same words of Job in his comment on Jeremiah 31, where the blind and the lame return from exile. He says their companions will be ready to help them, will be eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, as good Christians ought to be to one another on their way to heaven, and he cites Job 29:15. For Henry, being 'eyes to the blind' is something companions do for one another on a journey.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Jeremiah 31

evidence.quote: There companions will be ready to help them, will be eyes to the blind and legs to the lame, as good Christians ought to be to one another in their travels heavenward, Job xxix. 15.

job-29-15.caution: Henry is writing about companions helping one another on a journey, not about a person of standing helping the blind.

job-29-15.text: Matthew Henry, commenting on Proverbs, adds that it is more charity to counsel the poor than to counsel a prince, 'as Job was with his wisdom', and he cites Job 29:15 for it. Taken with his comment on Job itself, he consistently treats Job's help to the blind as the gift of wisdom and counsel rather than of alms.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Proverbs 1

evidence.quote: It is more dignity indeed to be counsellor to the prince, but it is more charity to be counsellor to the poor, as Job was with his wisdom. Job xxix. 15, I was eyes to the blind.

job-29-15.caution: Interpretation by Henry. The Hebrew of Job 29:15 is not discussed on the shelf.

job-29-15.text: The Law, as the 1915 Bible encyclopedia summarises it, specially enjoined care of the blind (Leviticus 19:14), and treated offences against them as breaches of the Law (Deuteronomy 27:18). Smith's Dictionary likewise says the Jews were specially charged to treat the blind with compassion and care. These are the commands that Job's claim sits beside: he describes himself as keeping and going beyond them.
job-29-15.source: International Standard Bible Encyclopaedia (1915), entry 'Blindness'; Smith's Bible Dictionary, entry 'Blindness'

evidence.quote: but care of the blind was specially enjoined in the Law (Lev 19 14), and offences against them are regarded as breaches of Law (Dt 27 18).
The Jews were specially charged to treat the blind with compassion and care.

job-29-15.caution: The last sentence of the text is the writer's link between the Law and Job; neither source mentions Job in these entries.

job-29-15.text: Matthew Henry describes the whole of Job's care in this chapter. He says Job was 'a father to the poor', counselling, directing and acting for them, and adds that 'it is no disparagement to the son of a prince to be a father to the poor'. He lists those Job helped: the poor who cried, the fatherless, those ready to perish, widows, and 'those that were upon any account at a loss', which is where he puts the blind and the lame.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Job 29

evidence.quote: It is no disparagement to the son of a prince to be a father to the poor.
(3.) Those that were ready to perish he saved from perishing, relieving those that were hungry and ready to perish for want

job-29-15.caution: Henry's list of the kinds of people Job helped is his own organisation of verses 11-17.

job-29-15.text: Matthew Henry notes where Job did this work. He says Job went out 'through the city' to the business at the gate, and that judgment was administered in the gate and in the street, in places of concourse to which every man might have free access. Smith's Dictionary agrees that city gates were used as places of public deliberation and the administration of justice.
job-29-15.source: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Job 29; Smith's Bible Dictionary, entry 'Gate'

evidence.quote: Observe, Judgment was administered in the gate, in the street, in the places of concourse, to which every man might have a free access
Places for public deliberation, administration of Justice, or of audience for kings and rulers or ambassadors.

job-29-15.caution: Smith's list is for gates of eastern cities generally.

job-29-15.text: Smith's Dictionary says Job lived in the land of Uz, which marks him as belonging to an Aramean branch that had settled south or south-east of Palestine, and that he is shown as a chieftain of immense wealth and high rank. Smith's adds that his worship was of the early patriarchal type and 'thoroughly domestic in form and spirit'.

evidence.quote: Job is represented as a chieftain of immense wealth and high rank, blameless in all the relations of life.
His residence in the land of Uz marks him as belonging to a branch of the Aramean race

job-29-15.caution: Smith's treats the book's date and nature as uncertain and notes opinions that it is history, fiction or a composition based on facts.

siloam-walk.text: Two modern figures are given for the climb between the Pool of Siloam and the Temple Mount: a rise of about 115 metres over a straight-line distance of about 634 metres. The same source gives the pool an elevation of about 625 metres and the Temple Mount a mean elevation of 740 metres, and calls the pool the lowest place within the historical city. The man in John 9 would have gone down this slope to the pool and had to climb back up it.
siloam-walk.source: Wikipedia, 'Pool of Siloam', revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0), citing Itzhaki, Israel Guide: Jerusalem (1980)

evidence.quote: the Pool of Siloam is the lowest place in altitude within the historical city of Jerusalem, with an elevation of about {{convert|625|m|ft|}} above sea level.
a [[Grade (slope)|gradient]] of {{convert|115|m|ft|}} in altitude at a linear distance of about {{convert|634|m}}, with a mean elevation in the Temple Mount of {{convert|740|m|ft|}} above sea level.

siloam-walk.caution: Modern measurements of the ground. The 634 metres is a straight line, not the length of any particular walking route.

siloam-walk.text: Josephus describes the ground between the Temple and Siloam. The valley of the Cheesemongers ran between the upper city and the lower city as far as Siloam, and the outer sides of the hills were ringed by deep valleys with precipices. He adds that the Hasmonean rulers had filled in an older valley to join the city to the temple. The route to the pool therefore ran down a built-up valley, with steep ground on both sides.
siloam-walk.source: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews, Book V, chapter 4, section 1 (Whiston translation)

evidence.quote: Now the Valley of the Cheesemongers, as it was called, and was that which we told you before distinguished the hill of the upper city from that of the lower, extended as far as Siloam; for that is the name of a fountain which hath sweet water in it, and this in great plenty also.
they filled up that valley with earth, and had a mind to join the city to the temple.

siloam-walk.caution: Whiston's 18th-century translation. Josephus describes the city as it stood shortly before AD 70, a generation after John 9.

siloam-walk.text: Edersheim describes the route of the priest's procession to Siloam at the Feast of Tabernacles. It went, he says, probably through Ophel, which he says was covered with buildings to the very edge of Siloam, down the edge of the Tyropoeon Valley where it meets the Kedron valley, to the Fountain-Gate and the Pool of Siloam, which he places still within the city wall. The priest then returned to the Temple through the Water-gate.
siloam-walk.source: Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, Book IV, chapter VII

evidence.quote: Onwards it passed, probably, through Ophel, which recent investigations have shown to have been covered with buildings to the very verge of Siloam, down the edge of the Tyropoeon Valley, where it merges into that of the Kedron.
Here was the so-called Fountain-Gate,' and still within the City-wall the Pool of Siloam,' the overflow of which fed a lower pool.
A threefold blast of the Priests' trumpets welcomed the arrival of the Priest, as he entered through the Water-gate,'

siloam-walk.caution: Edersheim's route is his own reconstruction (he says 'probably') for a ceremonial procession, not a record of the route in John 9. A 2006 news report quoted in Wikipedia places the pool outside the city wall; Edersheim places it inside.

siloam-walk.text: Archaeologists working in the 1880s recorded a stairway of 34 rock-hewn steps to the west of the pool, leading up from a court in front of it. Excavations after 2004 found the Second Temple period pool: stone-lined, slightly trapezoid, with steps on at least three sides in sets of five, which has been suggested as a way to cope with changing water levels. For a man who could not see, the main thing to picture is that the way down to the water was a staircase.
siloam-walk.source: Wikipedia, 'Pool of Siloam', revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.quote: there was a stairway of 34 rock-hewn steps to the west of the Pool of Siloam leading up from a court in front of the Pool of Siloam.

steps existed on at least three sides of the pool. The pool is not perfectly rectangular, but a soft [[trapezoid]]. There are three sets of five steps, two leading to a platform, before the bottom is reached, and it has been suggested that the steps were designed to accommodate various water levels.

siloam-walk.caution: The article summarises excavation reports. The 34 steps were recorded by 1880s excavators; the article does not say they belong to the Second Temple period pool.

siloam-walk.text: A news report of the 2000s excavation, quoted in a footnote of the Wikipedia article, says the excavators found a tiled road that ends at the pool and has its origins near the Temple Mount, and takes it to be the road worshippers used between the pool and the Temple. The article also says the pool was used by pilgrims for ritual purification before visiting the Temple enclosure.
siloam-walk.source: Wikipedia, 'Pool of Siloam', revision of 20 June 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0), quoting a Jerusalem Post report of 26 January 2006

evidence.quote: a tiled road which ends at the pool and has its origins near the Temple Mount. Ostensibly, this is the road that worshippers used to go back and forth between the Shiloah Pool and the Temple Mount.
The Pool of Siloam (perhaps referring to the Lower Pool) was used by pilgrims for [[ritual purification]] before visiting the Temple enclosure.

siloam-walk.caution: The road is the excavators' interpretation as reported by a newspaper; the word 'ostensibly' is in the quoted report.

siloam-walk.text: Smith's Dictionary describes how the pool was fed. A rock-cut conduit 1,708 feet long carries the water from the Virgin's fountain to Siloam, entering a small rock-cut chamber that is reached by a few rude steps. It measures a later pool at about 52 feet by 18 feet and 19 feet deep, and says that pool is not the original building and may be the work of the Crusaders.

evidence.quote: This conduit is 1708 feet long
To this you descend by a few rude steps
This pool is oblong, about 52 feet long, 18 feet broad and 19 feet deep
The present pool is not the original building; it may be the work of crusaders

siloam-walk.caution: 1863 text describing a later pool that excavation has since shown is not the Second Temple pool. Use it for the water supply, not for the pool Jesus used.

siloam-walk.text: Josephus describes the royal cloister of the Temple, which ran from the east valley to the west one. The valley beneath it was so deep that a person looking down from the battlements would be giddy, because the cloister stood on top of the height of the valley wall. The Temple area was a platform raised high above the valley around it.
siloam-walk.source: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book XV, chapter 11, section 5 (Whiston translation)

evidence.quote: while the valley was very deep, and its bottom could not be seen, if you looked from above into the depth, this further vastly high elevation of the cloister stood upon that height

siloam-walk.caution: Josephus, writing for Roman readers, is fond of superlatives. Josephus only says the valley was deep beneath the cloister.

siloam-walk.text: Josephus describes the old wall of Jerusalem as going south on the west side and 'having its bending above the fountain Siloam', then turning east towards Solomon's pool and on to Ophlas, where it joined the eastern cloister of the temple. Edersheim says the same: the oldest wall ran round the west of the Upper City, crossed south to the Pool of Siloam, then ran up east round Ophel until it reached the eastern enclosure of the Temple. On both accounts, Siloam sat at the south-east end of the old city, near the line of the wall below the Temple.
siloam-walk.source: Josephus, The Wars of the Jews, Book V, chapter 4 (Whiston translation); Edersheim, The Life and Times of Jesus the Messiah, Book II, chapter I

evidence.quote: after that it went southward, having its bending above the fountain Siloam, where it also bends again towards the east at Solomon's pool, and reaches as far as a certain place which they called "Ophlas," where it was joined to the eastern cloister of the temple.
then crossed south to the Pool of Siloam, and ran up east, round Ophel, till it reached the eastern enclosure of the Temple

siloam-walk.caution: Both describe the course of the oldest wall; neither says where the pool stood in relation to the wall in Jesus's day (compare the Edersheim item above and the Wikipedia caption that places the pool outside the wall).

siloam-walk.text: Wikipedia says that when Herod rebuilt the Temple he expanded the Temple Mount enclosure from 7 to 14.4 hectares, doubling it, and that above the Huldah Gates on top of the Temple walls stood the Royal Stoa, a hall of 162 columns in four rows. It also says water drawn from the Pool of Siloam was poured by the priest at the altar each day of the water libation ritual. These details set the Temple as a very large enclosure, with a link to the pool through the water ceremony.
siloam-walk.source: Wikipedia, 'Second Temple', revision of 19 September 2026 (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.quote: the Temple Mount complex initially measured {{convert|7|ha}} in size, but Herod expanded it to {{convert|14.4|ha}} and so doubled its area.
Above the [[Huldah Gates]], on top the Temple walls, was the [[Royal Stoa (Jerusalem)|Royal Stoa]], a large [[basilica]]
The water libation ritual, symbolizing the onset of the rainy season, involved water drawn from the [[Pool of Siloam]] and poured by the priest at the altar each day.

siloam-walk.caution: The water-libation detail is stated for the Feast of Tabernacles in the surrounding text, and 'each day' applies to that feast. The last sentence of the text is the writer's, and 'raised' follows Josephus (see above), not Wikipedia.
